explanations.answer: If Peter loves Him more than these
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jesus asks, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” The passage doesn't spell out what “these” means, so I'll leave it open too. Simon Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, doesn't get a warm-up question or a pat on the back first. I think a question that short and that direct makes a man stand up straight.

explanations.answer: If Peter will keep fishing with them
explanations.explanation: Nothing about fishing comes out of Jesus' mouth here. Breakfast is done, and He goes straight to the heart of it. He asks, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” No small talk about nets, no weather report, just one question. I've had plenty of conversations that went around the block first, but this one doesn't.

explanations.answer: If Peter knows who He really is
explanations.explanation: Jesus isn't quizzing Peter on who He is. He asks about Peter's love: “Do you love Me more than these?” Peter answers, “Yes, Lord,” and then, “You know I love You.” So the question is about the heart, not about passing a test. Good thing too, because I'd have sweated through my apron.

Yes, that's how it goes. After Peter answers the second time, Jesus tells him, “Shepherd My sheep.” Peter gets another job, not a lecture. I think that tells you something about how Jesus handles a man who says he loves Him: He gives him something to do.

It's actually true. After the second question, Jesus tells Peter, “Shepherd My sheep.” The job doesn't go away just because the question came back around. Peter answers the same way both times, and Jesus answers him with work both times.

That's it. The text says Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” It doesn't tell us why, and I won't guess past what it says. Peter doesn't storm off, though. He answers, “Lord, You know all things,” and, “You know I love You.”

Nobody's chuckling in this scene, baker. The passage says Peter was deeply hurt by the third question. I think the whole beach got pretty quiet. Even so, he answers Jesus honestly: “You know I love You.”

Relief would be a nice feeling, but it isn't the one in the text. John 21:17 says Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time. A third round of the same question stings, and the passage says so plainly. Peter still tells Him, “Lord, You know all things.”

explanations.answer: Where he does not want to go
explanations.explanation: That's right. Jesus says someone else will dress Peter and lead him “where you do not want to go.” It's a quiet line with a lot packed in. Young Peter walked wherever he wanted, and old Peter won't get to choose. I think this is one of the heavier parts of the passage, so take it slow.

explanations.answer: Wherever he asks them to go
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Jesus says. When Peter is old, someone else will dress him and lead him where he does not want to go. The young Peter is the one who walked where he wanted. Nobody in this picture is taking requests.

explanations.answer: Back home to his own boat
explanations.explanation: There's no boat in this part of Jesus' words. He says someone else will lead Peter “where you do not want to go.” A trip home to his own boat sounds like a place he'd want to go. I'd have picked it too, friend, but that's not what the text says.

Yes. John explains that Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. The writer tells us right there what the words are pointing to. It's a heavy thing to hear, and I won't joke about it. Then Jesus says to Peter, “Follow Me.”

It's true. The text says Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. So the words about old age aren't random. John tells us what they point to. It's a heavy moment, and right after it Jesus tells Peter, “Follow Me.”

That's the word. After Jesus finishes, He tells Peter, “Follow Me.” Short and simple, with no speech attached. Jesus uses the same two words again a few verses later, and I'll get to that when we meet them.

Jesus doesn't ask Peter to remember anything here. After talking about Peter's old age, He says, “Follow Me.” That's a word you do, not a word you hold onto. I forget where I put my own mustache wax half the time, so I'm glad He kept it that easy.

The word in the text isn't worship. After talking about Peter's old age, Jesus tells him, “Follow Me.” It's a call to walk behind Him, plain and direct. Peter hears it, and it sets up what happens next.

That's what Peter asks: “Lord, what about him?” He turns around, spots the disciple whom Jesus loved, and the question just comes out. I think we've all done that, glancing at the next person's plate when we should look at our own. Jesus answers him directly, and that answer is coming up.

Peter doesn't ask for anybody to join them. He sees the other disciple following and asks, “Lord, what about him?” That's a question about what's ahead for the other man, not an invitation. The text doesn't say what Peter had in mind, so I won't guess.

That would've been a fine question, but it's not the one Peter asks. He sees the disciple whom Jesus loved and says, “Lord, what about him?” Jesus is the one who asked about love, three times. Peter's question points at the other man, not at love.

Right. The rumor spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die. The brothers here are fellow believers. The rumor grew out of Jesus' answer, and the text sets it straight right away. Rumors can really travel, can't they?

Marriage never comes up in this passage. The rumor among the brothers was that this disciple would not die. That's a much bigger claim than a wedding. It took off from Jesus' answer to Peter, and John corrects it in the very next breath.

Preaching isn't what the rumor was about. The text says the rumor among the brothers was that this disciple would not die. The brothers here are fellow believers. It grew out of what Jesus said to Peter, and John corrects it himself.

Not quite. The text says Jesus did not say that this disciple would not die. What He said was, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?” The rumor took a question with an “if” in it and treated it like a promise. It's like a group chat that turns “maybe” into “definitely” by the third message.

That's right. John says plainly that Jesus did not say this disciple would not die. He said only, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?” The “if” got dropped somewhere between the brothers. A rumor can lose a whole word and still sound like the truth.

Correct. John 21:24 says, “This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down.” That's the same disciple Peter turned around and saw following them. Then the passage adds, “And we know that his testimony is true.” He wrote it all down, and the rumor corrected itself right on the page.

Peter is the one Jesus was talking to, but he's not the one the passage names as the writer. Verse 24 points to the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one Peter asked about. Peter was busy asking questions, and the other disciple was busy taking notes. Good thing somebody was.

Thomas, called Didymus, is one of the disciples listed on the beach with the others (John 21:2). But this passage never names him as the writer. Verse 24 says the one who testifies and wrote these things down is the disciple whom Jesus loved. I'd love to hand out a gold star for the guess, but the text points elsewhere.
